q: What is the capital of Spain?
fact: Madrid sits near the centre of Spain and is one of Europe's highest capital cities.

q: What is the capital of Germany?
fact: Berlin's Brandenburg Gate is topped by a statue of a chariot pulled by four horses.

q: In which city would you find the Colosseum?
fact: The Colosseum could hold an estimated 50,000 or more spectators.

q: Which country's flag is white with a red circle in the middle?
fact: Japan is made up of thousands of islands, and the biggest of them, Honshu, is home to Tokyo.

q: Which is the largest ocean in the world?
fact: The Pacific covers more of Earth's surface than all the land on the planet put together.

q: Kenya is in which continent?
fact: Kenya takes its name from Mount Kenya, the second-highest mountain in Africa.

q: Which country has a red maple leaf on its flag?
fact: Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world.

q: In which country are the Pyramids of Giza?
fact: The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years.

q: Which US city is nicknamed 'the Big Apple'?
fact: New York's Central Park is larger than the whole of Monaco.

q: Hollywood, the home of the US film industry, is in which city?
fact: The famous Hollywood sign originally read 'Hollywoodland' and advertised new houses.

q: In which country would you find the Great Wall?
fact: The Great Wall isn't one single wall but a series of walls built over many centuries.

q: In which country is the Taj Mahal?
fact: The Taj Mahal stands on the bank of the Yamuna river in the city of Agra.

q: Lisbon is the capital city of which country?
fact: Lisbon is famous for its old yellow trams that rattle up and down its steep hills.

q: Which is the largest continent?
fact: Around six in every ten people in the world live in Asia.

q: Which Italian city is famous for its canals and gondolas?
fact: Venice is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon.

q: What is the capital of Greece?
fact: Athens is one of the world's oldest cities, with a recorded history of more than 3,000 years.

q: Which sea lies between southern Europe and North Africa?
fact: The name 'Mediterranean' comes from Latin words meaning 'in the middle of the land'.

q: Which famous river flows through Egypt?
fact: The Nile flows north and ends in a wide, fan-shaped delta on the Mediterranean coast.

q: Which country borders the USA to the south?
fact: Mexico City is built on the bed of an old lake, and parts of it are slowly sinking.

q: Copenhagen is the capital of which country?
fact: Copenhagen's Little Mermaid statue was inspired by a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.

q: What is the name of the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth?
fact: The Equator passes through Brazil, Kenya and Indonesia, among other countries.

q: The city of Rio de Janeiro is in which country?
fact: Rio de Janeiro means 'River of January' in Portuguese.

q: What is the capital city of the USA?
fact: The 'D.C.' in Washington, D.C. stands for District of Columbia.

q: Argentina is in which continent?
fact: Argentina's name comes from 'argentum', the Latin word for silver.

q: On which continent is the South Pole?
fact: Antarctica is the only continent with no permanent human residents.

q: Which ocean lies between Europe and North America?
fact: The Atlantic Ocean is getting a few centimetres wider every year.

q: Which Scandinavian country is famous for its fjords?
fact: In the far north of Norway, the summer sun doesn't set for weeks, known as the midnight sun.

q: What is the capital of Russia?
fact: Moscow's metro is famous for grand stations decorated with chandeliers and mosaics.

q: Amsterdam is the capital of which country?
fact: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by dykes and dunes.

q: Which US state is made up entirely of islands?
fact: Hawaii's islands were formed by volcanoes, and some of those volcanoes are still active.

q: What is the capital of China?
fact: Beijing's Forbidden City was the palace of Chinese emperors for almost 500 years.

q: Mount Everest is in which mountain range?
fact: The name Himalaya comes from Sanskrit words meaning 'abode of snow'.

q: What do we call a piece of land completely surrounded by water?
fact: Greenland is the world's largest island that isn't counted as a continent.

q: Brussels is the capital of which country?
fact: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.

q: What is the capital of the Republic of Ireland?
fact: Dublin's name comes from the Irish 'Dubh Linn', meaning 'black pool'.

q: Which famous queen of ancient Egypt was linked with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

q: Which Tudor queen was known as 'the Virgin Queen'?
fact: Elizabeth I spoke several languages, including French, Italian, Latin and Greek.

q: Which explorer famously sailed across the Atlantic to the Americas in 1492?
fact: Columbus was born in Genoa, in what is now Italy, but his famous voyage was paid for by Spain.

q: Gladiators performed in arenas in which ancient civilisation?
fact: Some gladiators were so popular that fans scratched graffiti about them onto walls in Pompeii.

q: Which seafarers from Scandinavia sailed in longships?
fact: There's no evidence Vikings wore horned helmets; that idea became popular in the 1800s.

q: What was the main language of the ancient Romans?
fact: Homo sapiens, the scientific name for humans, is Latin for 'wise man'.

q: Which famous nurse was known as 'the Lady with the Lamp'?
fact: Florence Nightingale was also a gifted statistician who used diagrams to present her findings.

q: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
fact: The word 'pharaoh' comes from an Egyptian term meaning 'great house', first used for the royal palace.

q: Which famous prehistoric stone circle stands on Salisbury Plain?
fact: Stonehenge's smaller 'bluestones' were brought about 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales.

q: Which scientist is said to have been inspired by a falling apple to think about gravity?
fact: Newton's famous apple tree still grows at Woolsthorpe Manor, his childhood home in Lincolnshire.

q: In medieval times, what was a large fortified home with a moat and drawbridge?
fact: Windsor Castle is said to be the oldest and largest occupied castle in the world.

q: Which Roman leader gave his name to the month of July?
fact: Before it was renamed, July was called Quintilis, meaning 'fifth month'.

q: What did the Romans build to carry fresh water into their towns?
fact: The Pont du Gard, a Roman aqueduct bridge in southern France, is nearly 50 metres tall.

q: According to legend, which king gathered his knights around a Round Table?
fact: In the legends, Arthur's court was at Camelot and his magical sword was called Excalibur.

q: In which forest is Robin Hood said to have lived?
fact: In the legends, Robin Hood's band of Merry Men included Little John and Friar Tuck.

q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
fact: Richard Arkwright's Cromford Mill in Derbyshire, begun in 1771, was one of the first modern factories.

q: Ancient Egyptians wrote on a paper-like material made from which plant?
fact: Our word 'paper' comes from 'papyrus', a reed that grew along the River Nile.

q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the USA as a gift?
fact: The Statue of Liberty was a shiny copper-brown colour at first and slowly turned green as it weathered.

q: The Penny Black was the world's first what?
fact: The Penny Black, issued in 1840, showed a side view of the young Queen Victoria.

q: Which ancient people built the Parthenon?
fact: The Parthenon's columns bulge very slightly in the middle so they look perfectly straight from afar.

q: What was the metal suit worn by medieval knights called?
fact: A full suit of plate armour usually weighed about 15 to 25 kg, spread across the whole body.

q: Which garment, a long draped piece of cloth, was worn by men in ancient Rome?
fact: Togas were usually made of wool and could be several metres long.

q: In Roman numerals, which number does X stand for?
fact: Roman numerals had no symbol for zero.

q: Which British monarch was the first to celebrate a Platinum Jubilee?
fact: A lemon Swiss roll and amaretti trifle won the Platinum Pudding competition for the 2022 Jubilee.

q: Which age came straight after the Stone Age?
fact: Bronze is made by mixing copper with a smaller amount of tin.

q: The Great Sphinx of Giza has the body of which animal?
fact: The Great Sphinx was carved out of a single mass of limestone bedrock.

q: The Model T was a famous early car made by which company?
fact: Henry Ford said customers could have a Model T in any colour 'so long as it is black'.

q: What is another name for the Middle Ages?
fact: 'Medieval' comes from the Latin 'medium aevum', meaning 'middle age'.

q: Which famous Paris landmark was built for the World's Fair of 1889?
fact: The Eiffel Tower was originally only meant to stand for 20 years.

q: Who was Queen Elizabeth II's husband?
fact: Elizabeth and Philip married at Westminster Abbey in 1947.

q: Which scientist came up with the theory of relativity?
fact: Einstein's most famous equation, E = mc², shows how energy and mass are linked.

q: Which country was once ruled by tsars?
fact: The word 'tsar' comes from 'Caesar', the title used by Roman emperors.

q: Samurai were the famous warriors of which country?
fact: Samurai often carried two swords: a long katana and a shorter one called a wakizashi.

q: Which Scottish scientist discovered penicillin?
fact: Fleming spotted penicillin in 1928 after mould grew on a dish he had left out in his lab.

q: Which famous playwright lived during the reign of Elizabeth I?
fact: Many of Shakespeare's plays were performed at the Globe, on the south bank of the Thames.

q: Which substance has the chemical formula H₂O?
fact: Water is one of the few substances that expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.

q: At what temperature in Celsius does water freeze?
fact: Adding salt to water lowers its freezing point, which is why roads are gritted with salt in winter.

q: Which force keeps our feet on the ground?
fact: On the Moon, gravity is about a sixth as strong, so you'd weigh about a sixth of what you do on Earth.

q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
fact: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times every day.

q: Which organs do we use to breathe?
fact: Your left lung is slightly smaller than your right, which leaves room for your heart.

q: Which gas do we need to breathe in to stay alive?
fact: Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air we breathe.

q: What does a thermometer measure?
fact: Normal human body temperature is about 37°C.

q: How many colours are traditionally listed in a rainbow?
fact: You can only see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and the rain is in front of you.

q: Which of these metals does a magnet attract?
fact: The Earth itself acts like a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.

q: Which bone protects your brain?
fact: A newborn baby's skull has soft gaps called fontanelles, which close up as they grow.

q: What would you use to look at tiny things like cells?
fact: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was among the first to see bacteria, using tiny home-made microscopes in the 1670s.

q: Light bulbs are labelled with their power in which unit?
fact: The watt is named after James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine.

q: Which vitamin does your skin make when it's in sunlight?
fact: Oily fish such as salmon and mackerel are among the few foods naturally rich in vitamin D.

q: What do solar panels turn sunlight into?
fact: Solar panels still make some electricity on cloudy days, just less than in full sunshine.

q: Which gas makes the bubbles in fizzy drinks?
fact: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water forms a weak acid, giving fizzy drinks their slight tang.

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
fact: Red blood cells get their colour from haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein.

q: What is the hard, white outer layer of a tooth called?
fact: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.

q: Which organs clean your blood and make urine?
fact: Most people have two kidneys, but you can live a healthy life with just one.

q: Which direction does a compass needle point?
fact: A compass points to magnetic north, which isn't quite the same place as the North Pole.

q: What is an echo?
fact: Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their way and hunt, a skill called echolocation.

q: Which of these travels fastest?
fact: Light travels so much faster than sound that you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

q: Sodium chloride is better known as what?
fact: Sodium on its own is a soft metal that reacts violently with water.

q: What is a scientist who studies rocks called?
fact: The word 'geology' comes from the Greek words for 'Earth' and 'study'.

q: Bread, rice and pasta are rich in which nutrient?
fact: Your body breaks carbohydrates down into glucose, its main source of quick energy.

q: Which joint connects your hand to your arm?
fact: Each wrist contains eight small bones called carpals.

q: Which force slows down an object sliding across a surface?
fact: Rubbing your hands together warms them up because friction turns movement into heat.

q: What is a material that lets electricity flow easily called?
fact: Plastic is an insulator, which is why electrical wires are wrapped in it.

q: Which metal are most household electrical wires made of?
fact: Of all metals, only silver conducts electricity better than copper.

q: Steam, or water vapour, is water in which state?
fact: True steam is invisible: the white cloud above a kettle is really tiny water droplets.

q: Which scientist is famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
fact: Darwin's ideas were shaped by his voyage on HMS Beagle, including a visit to the Galápagos Islands.

q: What is it called when water slowly turns into vapour, like a drying puddle?
fact: Puddles dry up faster on warm, windy days because evaporation speeds up.

q: In which part of the body would you find the retina?
fact: Images land on the retina upside down, and your brain flips them the right way up.

q: In a school science lab, what is a Bunsen burner used for?
fact: The Bunsen burner is named after German chemist Robert Bunsen, who helped make it popular in the 1850s.

q: Which gas is used to make party balloons float?
fact: Helium is the second most common element in the universe, after hydrogen.

q: Taste buds are mostly found on which part of your body?
fact: Your taste buds are constantly renewed, with each one lasting only a week or two.

q: How many legs does an insect have?
fact: Spiders aren't insects: they have eight legs and belong to a group called arachnids.

q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
fact: Inside its chrysalis, a caterpillar breaks down almost completely before rebuilding itself.

q: What is a baby frog called?
fact: Tadpoles breathe through gills, then develop lungs as they grow into frogs.

q: What is a baby cow called?
fact: Baby elephants, whales and giraffes are also called calves.

q: Which big cat is the male famous for his shaggy mane?
fact: A lion's roar can be heard up to about 8 kilometres away.

q: What do giant pandas mainly eat?
fact: A giant panda can spend 10 to 16 hours a day eating.

q: Which animal uses its long trunk to drink and grab food?
fact: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and no bones at all.

q: Which bird is famous for fanning out its colourful tail?
fact: Strictly, only males are peacocks: females are peahens, and together they're peafowl.

q: What colour is a robin's breast?
fact: Robins are one of the few UK birds that sing all through the winter.

q: Which lizard is famous for changing colour?
fact: A chameleon's eyes can move separately, so it can look in two directions at once.

q: What is the tallest animal in the world?
fact: A giraffe's tongue can be around 50 cm long and is dark in colour.

q: What is an animal that eats only plants called?
fact: Animals that eat both plants and meat, like bears and humans, are called omnivores.

q: Which sea creature has a hard shell and often walks sideways?
fact: A hermit crab doesn't grow its own shell; it moves into empty ones as it gets bigger.

q: Which garden creature carries a shell on its back?
fact: Snails make a slimy mucus that helps them glide along, even over sharp edges.

q: In which season do many trees drop their leaves?
fact: Leaves change colour as green chlorophyll breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments.

q: Which bird hoots and hunts at night?
fact: Owls can turn their heads around about 270 degrees.

q: Which African animal has black and white stripes?
fact: Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique, a bit like a human fingerprint.

q: What is it called when animals sleep through the winter?
fact: Hedgehogs, dormice and bats are among the UK animals that hibernate.

q: Which tall yellow flower is named after the Sun?
fact: Young sunflowers follow the Sun across the sky, but most fully grown ones face east.

q: Which sweet liquid do bees collect from flowers?
fact: Many bees carry pollen home in little 'baskets' on their back legs.

q: What is a male chicken called?
fact: A female chicken is called a hen, and a young female is called a pullet.

q: Which animal is famous for building dams across rivers?
fact: Beavers have orange teeth, coloured by iron that makes them extra strong.

q: What is a baby bear called?
fact: Lions, tigers and foxes also call their babies cubs.

q: Which part of a plant grows underground and soaks up water?
fact: Carrots, parsnips and beetroot are all roots that we eat.

q: What is a group of wolves called?
fact: Wolves howl to keep in touch with their pack, and a howl can carry for miles.

q: Which African animal is famous for its 'laughing' call?
fact: Despite looking a bit like dogs, hyenas are more closely related to cats and mongooses.

q: Which playful sea mammal talks using clicks and whistles?
fact: Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time, so they can keep surfacing to breathe.

q: What is a female deer called?
fact: A male deer is called a stag or a buck, and a baby deer is a fawn.

q: Which tree do acorns come from?
fact: A big oak tree can produce tens of thousands of acorns in a good year.

q: Which spring flower is famously grown in fields across the Netherlands?
fact: Tulips originally came from Central Asia and Turkey, not the Netherlands.

q: What colour are flamingos?
fact: Flamingos get their pink colour from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.

q: Which animal is nicknamed 'the ship of the desert'?
fact: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.

q: Which small beetle is usually red with black spots?
fact: A ladybird's bright colours warn birds that it tastes nasty.

q: What are small balls of ice that fall from storm clouds called?
fact: Hailstones grow in layers as they're tossed up and down inside storm clouds.

q: What is a baby goat called?
fact: Goats have rectangular pupils, which give them a very wide field of view.

q: What is the main ingredient of an omelette?
fact: A classic French omelette is cooked quickly and rolled so it stays soft inside.

q: Spaghetti bolognese is named after a city in which country?
fact: In Bologna itself, the traditional meat ragù is usually served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti.

q: What colour is the flesh of a typical ripe kiwi fruit?
fact: Kiwi fruit were once sold under the name Chinese gooseberries.

q: Which drink is made from roasted beans and can be served as an espresso?
fact: Coffee beans are actually the seeds of a small, cherry-like fruit.

q: Chips are usually made by cutting up which vegetable?
fact: Potatoes first came to Europe from South America in the 16th century.

q: Which fruit is dried to make raisins?
fact: Sultanas and currants are dried grapes too, just from different varieties.

q: What is the yellow part of an egg called?
fact: The colour of an egg yolk depends largely on what the hen has been eating.

q: Which country is famous for sushi?
fact: The word sushi refers to the seasoned vinegared rice, not the raw fish.

q: Which vegetable is traditionally carved into a lantern at Halloween?
fact: In Ireland and Scotland, people carved turnips long before pumpkins caught on.

q: Tofu is made from which kind of bean?
fact: Tofu is made by curdling soya milk, a bit like the way cheese is made.

q: According to the saying, which fruit a day keeps the doctor away?
fact: Thousands of different apple varieties are grown around the world.

q: Which drink is made by fermenting grapes?
fact: Sparkling wine can only be called Champagne if it comes from the Champagne region of France.

q: Alongside eggs and milk, what is the main ingredient of Yorkshire pudding batter?
fact: Yorkshire puddings were often served with gravy before the meat, to fill people up.

q: What kind of food is cheddar?
fact: Cheddar takes its name from a village in Somerset, near Cheddar Gorge.

q: Penne, fusilli and farfalle are all types of what?
fact: Farfalle means 'butterflies' in Italian, after its bow-tie shape.

q: Tacos and burritos are classic dishes from which country?
fact: Corn tortillas have been eaten in Mexico for thousands of years.

q: Which fruit has its seeds on the outside?
fact: Botanically, strawberries aren't true berries, but bananas are.

q: Tinned baked beans usually come in a sauce made from what?
fact: The beans in a tin of baked beans are usually haricot beans, also called navy beans.

q: Which hot drink, made from dried leaves, is often served with milk in Britain?
fact: Black, green and white teas all come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis.

q: Which long yellow fruit has a skin you peel before eating?
fact: A single banana is called a finger, and a bunch of them is called a hand.

q: Which fish is most commonly used for British fish and chips?
fact: Haddock is the other big favourite, especially in Scotland and the north of England.

q: Popcorn is made by heating the kernels of which plant?
fact: Popcorn pops because the water inside each kernel turns to steam and bursts it open.

q: Which vegetable is famous for making people cry when they chop it?
fact: Chilling an onion in the fridge before cutting it can help reduce the tears.

q: Along with sugar, what is the main ingredient of meringue?
fact: A pinch of cream of tartar helps whisked egg whites hold their shape.

q: Botanically speaking, is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?
fact: Tomatoes belong to the same plant family as potatoes and aubergines.

q: Which cheese is traditionally used on a margherita pizza?
fact: Mozzarella is stretched and kneaded in hot water, which gives it its stringy texture.

q: Chocolate is made from which beans?
fact: Cocoa pods grow straight out of the trunk and branches of the cacao tree.

q: Which fruit is most often used to make marmalade?
fact: Bitter Seville oranges are prized for marmalade because they set so well.

q: What is the traditional filling of a Cornish pasty?
fact: Genuine Cornish pasties have protected status and must be prepared in Cornwall.

q: Which meat is traditionally served with mint sauce?
fact: Mint sauce is usually made from chopped mint, vinegar and a little sugar.

q: Cider is traditionally made from which fruit?
fact: Perry is a similar drink made by fermenting pears instead of apples.

q: Which herb is the main ingredient of classic green pesto?
fact: Classic pesto comes from Genoa, in the Liguria region of north-west Italy.

q: Which large fruit has a hard, hairy shell and watery juice inside?
fact: Despite its name, a coconut is botanically a drupe rather than a true nut.

q: Which orange vegetable is said to help you see in the dark?
fact: Early cultivated carrots were often purple or yellow rather than orange.

q: The Victoria sponge cake is named after which British monarch?
fact: The Victoria sponge is also called a Victoria sandwich, as the jam is sandwiched between two cakes.

q: How many players does a netball team have on court?
fact: Each netball position wears a bib with letters, such as GS for Goal Shooter.

q: In which sport would you hit a home run?
fact: Rounders, often played in British schools, is a close relative of baseball.

q: In darts, what is the highest score possible with three darts?
fact: A 180 needs all three darts to land in the treble 20, the thin inner ring worth triple points.

q: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
fact: Players at Wimbledon must wear almost entirely white clothing.

q: How many players are in a rugby union team on the pitch?
fact: Rugby league is a little different, with 13 players on each side.

q: In which sport do players use a cue to pot balls?
fact: The highest possible break in snooker under normal play is 147.

q: In golf, what is a score of one under par on a hole called?
fact: Finishing a hole two under par is called an eagle.

q: What shape is a rugby ball?
fact: Early rugby balls were made from pigs' bladders covered in leather.

q: How many players does each basketball team have on court?
fact: Basketball was invented in 1891 using peach baskets as the hoops.

q: The Grand National is a famous event in which sport?
fact: The Grand National is held at Aintree Racecourse, near Liverpool.

q: In chess, which piece must you protect to avoid losing the game?
fact: The queen is the most powerful piece, able to move any distance in a straight line in any direction.

q: In which sport do players hit a puck?
fact: Ice hockey pucks are usually frozen before games so that they bounce less.

q: Lord's in London is a world-famous ground for which sport?
fact: Lord's is often called the 'Home of Cricket'.

q: Which board game features properties, houses and hotels?
fact: On a Monopoly board, the Free Parking corner sits diagonally opposite Go.

q: In boxing, what does KO stand for?
fact: Despite being called a ring, a boxing ring is actually square.

q: Which flag is waved to show the end of a Formula 1 race?
fact: A red flag in Formula 1 means the session has been stopped.

q: How often are the Summer Olympic Games normally held?
fact: Since 1994, the Summer and Winter Games have been held two years apart.

q: In which sport do you try to knock down ten pins with a ball?
fact: A perfect game in ten-pin bowling scores 300 points.

q: In football, what colour card means a player is sent off?
fact: Red and yellow cards were introduced at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.

q: Which water sport involves riding waves while standing on a board?
fact: Surfing made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games.

q: Usain Bolt is famous for which sport?
fact: Usain Bolt comes from Jamaica, and his famous nickname is 'Lightning Bolt'.

q: In tennis, what is a serve called that the opponent fails to touch?
fact: If a serve clips the net and still lands in, it's called a let and is replayed.

q: In which sport would you race around a velodrome?
fact: Velodrome tracks are steeply banked so riders can take the bends at speed.

q: In cricket, how many balls are bowled in a standard over?
fact: An over in which the bowler gives away no runs is called a maiden.

q: Which sport is played on horseback using long mallets?
fact: A polo match is divided into periods called chukkas.

q: In which card game do you try to get as close to 21 as possible?
fact: In the UK, a similar game is often called pontoon.

q: Which swimming stroke is done lying on your back?
fact: Backstroke swimmers start their races in the water, holding on to the starting block.

q: Which city hosted the 2012 Summer Olympics?
fact: London was the first city to host the Summer Olympics three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

q: What is the official in charge of a football match called?
fact: The assistant referees who run the touchlines used to be called linesmen.

q: In which sport would you perform on a balance beam?
fact: The balance beam used in gymnastics is just 10 centimetres wide.

q: In which sport do teams hit a ball over a high net using their hands?
fact: Beach volleyball is played in teams of just two players.

q: In which kind of race do runners pass a baton to teammates?
fact: In a sprint relay, the baton must be passed within a marked exchange zone.

q: In which winter sport do you ride down a slope on a single wide board?
fact: Snowboarding first became an Olympic sport at the 1998 Nagano Winter Games.

q: Which garden game involves hitting balls through hoops with a mallet?
fact: Croquet was one of the sports played at the 1900 Paris Olympics.

q: The Ryder Cup is a famous competition in which sport?
fact: The Ryder Cup is played between teams from Europe and the United States.

q: Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
fact: Rowling first had the idea for Harry Potter on a delayed train from Manchester to London in 1990.

q: Who wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory?
fact: As a schoolboy, Roald Dahl helped taste-test new chocolate bars sent to his school by Cadbury.

q: Which Shakespeare play is about a prince of Denmark?
fact: Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play, and uncut performances can last around four hours.

q: In Disney's Frozen, what is the name of Elsa's younger sister?
fact: Frozen was loosely inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale The Snow Queen.

q: What is the name of the young lion in The Lion King?
fact: 'Simba' is the Swahili word for 'lion'.

q: Which superhero is secretly the billionaire Bruce Wayne?
fact: Batman first appeared in the American comic book Detective Comics in 1939.

q: Which superhero is secretly Peter Parker?
fact: Spider-Man first swung into comics in 1962, in an issue of Amazing Fantasy.

q: How many dwarfs does Snow White meet in the Disney film?
fact: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) was Disney's first full-length animated feature film.

q: In which city is the Louvre museum?
fact: The Louvre's famous glass pyramid entrance was designed by the architect I. M. Pei and opened in 1989.

q: Which musical instrument usually has 88 black and white keys?
fact: The piano's full name, 'pianoforte', means 'soft-loud' in Italian.

q: How many strings does a standard violin have?
fact: A violin bow is traditionally strung with horsehair.

q: Which band were nicknamed the Fab Four?
fact: The Beatles recorded most of their music at Abbey Road Studios in London.

q: Which author created Peter Rabbit?
fact: Beatrix Potter loved the Lake District and left much of her land there to the National Trust.

q: Which film features a giant shark menacing the seaside town of Amity?
fact: The mechanical shark used to film Jaws was nicknamed 'Bruce' by the crew.

q: Which fictional spy is known by the code number 007?
fact: Ian Fleming borrowed the name James Bond from an American expert on birds.

q: Who wrote A Christmas Carol?
fact: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks, and it was published in December 1843.

q: What is the name of the cowboy doll in Toy Story?
fact: Toy Story (1995) was the first feature film made entirely with computer animation.

q: What colour do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
fact: Painters have traditionally been taught that red, yellow and blue are the three primary colours.

q: Which Shakespeare play features three witches and a Scottish nobleman?
fact: Superstitious actors avoid saying this play's name inside a theatre and call it 'the Scottish Play'.

q: In which town was William Shakespeare born?
fact: You can still visit the house on Henley Street where Shakespeare is believed to have been born.

q: Children reach which magical land through a wardrobe in C.S. Lewis's famous book?
fact: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe was first published in 1950.

q: Which Disney film stars a mermaid called Ariel?
fact: Ariel's best friend in the film is a little fish called Flounder.

q: In The Wizard of Oz, what does the Tin Man hope to get from the Wizard?
fact: His travelling companions are the Scarecrow, who wants a brain, and the Cowardly Lion, who wants courage.

q: Which Dickens orphan famously asks for more food?
fact: Oliver Twist was turned into the hit stage musical Oliver!, which later became a film.

q: Which author wrote the Famous Five books?
fact: Enid Blyton was incredibly productive and wrote hundreds of books during her career.

q: Which green ogre starred in a hit 2001 animated film?
fact: Shrek is based on a 1990 picture book by the American author and cartoonist William Steig.

q: Who wrote The Lord of the Rings?
fact: Tolkien was a professor of English language and literature at Oxford University.

q: In Finding Nemo, what kind of fish is Nemo?
fact: Real clownfish live among sea anemones, protected from their stings by a special coat of mucus.

q: What is the famous nickname of the Academy Award statuette?
fact: Each Oscar statuette is made of bronze and plated in 24-carat gold.

q: Which author wrote Emma and Sense and Sensibility?
fact: Austen's first published novel didn't carry her name - it was credited simply to 'A Lady'.

q: Who wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
fact: Lewis Carroll was a pen name - the author's real name was Charles Lutwidge Dodgson.

q: Which famous Agatha Christie detective is Belgian?
fact: Poirot is famous for his neat moustache and for relying on his 'little grey cells'.

q: In The Jungle Book, what kind of animal is Baloo?
fact: The Jungle Book stories were written by Rudyard Kipling and first published in 1894.

q: Which famous marble statue of a young man did Michelangelo carve?
fact: Michelangelo's David was carved from a single huge block of marble and stands in Florence.

q: The musical Mamma Mia! is built around the songs of which band?
fact: ABBA's name is made from the first letters of the four band members' first names.

q: What do you call a word that means the same as another word?
fact: A thesaurus is a book of synonyms, and its name comes from a Greek word for 'treasure house'.

q: What do you call a word that means the opposite of another word?
fact: 'Antonym' comes from the Greek for 'against' and 'name'.

q: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
fact: Words now spelt with a J, like 'jest', were once often written with an I instead.

q: Which letter comes first in the Greek alphabet?
fact: The English word 'alphabet' comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters.

q: What are the letters A, E, I, O and U known as?
fact: 'Strengths' is a nine-letter English word with only one vowel.

q: In grammar, what is a 'doing' word called?
fact: The word 'verb' comes from the Latin 'verbum', which simply means 'word'.

q: Which type of word describes a noun, like 'tall' or 'blue'?
fact: In English, adjectives usually go before the noun, but in French they often come after it.

q: In 'The dog barked loudly', which word is an adverb?
fact: Many English adverbs are made by adding '-ly' to an adjective, like 'quick' becoming 'quickly'.

q: What does the French word 'bonjour' mean?
fact: 'Bonjour' joins 'bon', meaning good, and 'jour', meaning day.

q: What does the Spanish word 'gracias' mean?
fact: Spanish is an official language in around 20 countries, from Spain to most of South America.

q: Which language gave English the words 'pizza' and 'spaghetti'?
fact: 'Spaghetti' comes from the Italian for 'little strings'.

q: Which punctuation mark goes at the end of a question?
fact: In Spanish, a written question also starts with an upside-down question mark: ¿

q: What does BBC stand for?
fact: The BBC began life in 1922 as the British Broadcasting Company, before becoming a corporation.

q: If an invitation says 'RSVP', what are you being asked to do?
fact: RSVP stands for the French phrase 'répondez s'il vous plaît', meaning 'please reply'.

q: What does 'e.g.' mean?
fact: 'e.g.' is short for the Latin 'exempli gratia', meaning 'for the sake of example'.

q: What does 'P.S.' at the end of a letter stand for?
fact: 'Postscript' comes from the Latin 'post scriptum', meaning 'written after'.

q: 'Listen' and 'silent' use the same letters. What is this called?
fact: With a little rearranging, the letters of 'dormitory' spell 'dirty room'.

q: What is the past tense of 'run'?
fact: The word 'run' has hundreds of different senses listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

q: What are words like 'sea' and 'see', which sound the same but mean different things?
fact: 'Homophone' comes from the Greek for 'same sound'.

q: In the word 'unhappy', what is 'un-' called?
fact: Prefixes go at the start of a word, while suffixes such as '-ness' go at the end.

q: What do you call a word like 'he', 'she' or 'they' that stands in for a noun?
fact: Words like 'and', 'but' and 'or', which join parts of a sentence, are called conjunctions.

q: Which word means 'very large'?
fact: 'Enormous' comes from Latin meaning 'out of the norm' - something unusually big.

q: What is the plural of 'goose'?
fact: A group of geese on the ground is called a gaggle.

q: Which of these is spelt correctly?
fact: A handy tip: 'necessary' has one collar and two sleeves - one C and two S's.

q: What do you call a shortened form of a word, like 'Dr' for 'Doctor'?
fact: Rather amusingly, 'abbreviation' is itself quite a long word.

q: What does 'tri-' mean in words like 'tricycle' and 'triangle'?
fact: A triathlon combines three sports: swimming, cycling and running.

q: What does 'centi-' mean in the word 'centipede'?
fact: Despite the name, no centipede has exactly 100 legs - they always have an odd number of pairs.

q: What does 'aqua' mean in words like 'aquarium'?
fact: The star sign Aquarius is known as the water-bearer.

q: In text messages, what does 'LOL' usually stand for?
fact: 'LOL' was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2011, along with 'OMG'.

q: Which language is spoken alongside English in Wales?
fact: Road signs in Wales show place names in both Welsh and English.

q: A haiku is a short form of poem from which country?
fact: A traditional haiku has three lines of five, seven and five syllables.

q: Which letter is silent in the word 'knee'?
fact: The 'k' in words like 'knee' and 'knight' was actually pronounced in Old English.

q: Which of these is a compound word, made from two smaller words?
fact: Compound words can be joined like 'football', hyphenated like 'mother-in-law' or open like 'ice cream'.

q: What do you call the bad character in a story?
fact: In medieval times a 'villain' (or villein) was simply a farm worker tied to a lord's land.

q: What word describes someone who speaks two languages fluently?
fact: 'Bilingual' comes from the Latin 'bi' (two) and 'lingua', meaning tongue.

q: What do we call a person trained to travel into space?
fact: The word astronaut comes from Greek words meaning 'star sailor'.

q: What type of object is the Sun?
fact: The Sun is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it.

q: Which planet is third from the Sun?
fact: Earth is the only planet known to have liquid water on its surface.

q: What is it called when the Moon blocks our view of the Sun during the day?
fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

q: What does ISS stand for in space travel?
fact: The International Space Station zooms all the way around Earth roughly every 90 minutes.

q: NASA is the space agency of which country?
fact: NASA was set up in 1958, more than a decade before the first Moon landing.

q: What is a 'shooting star' really?
fact: Most shooting stars are made by specks of space dust no bigger than a grain of sand.

q: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
fact: Isaac Newton's ideas about gravity are said to have been inspired by a falling apple.

q: What do we call a group of stars that forms a pattern or picture in the sky?
fact: Astronomers officially recognise 88 constellations covering the whole sky.

q: Roughly how long does it take Earth to travel once around the Sun?
fact: A year is about 365 and a quarter days, which is why we add an extra day every leap year.

q: Roughly how long does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
fact: Earth's spin is very gradually slowing down, so days were shorter when dinosaurs lived.

q: What is the name for a scientist who studies stars and planets?
fact: The Royal Observatory in Greenwich was founded for astronomers in 1675.

q: What is an icy space object that grows a glowing tail as it nears the Sun?
fact: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed back by sunlight and the solar wind.

q: What are the rocky objects that mostly orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter?
fact: Some asteroids even have their own tiny moons orbiting them.

q: Which planet is named after the king of the Roman gods?
fact: Jupiter is so big that all the other planets in the Solar System could fit inside it.

q: In 1969, the Apollo 11 mission landed astronauts where?
fact: The Apollo 11 crew brought back about 21 kilograms of Moon rock and dust.

q: What do astronomers use to make distant stars and planets look bigger?
fact: Galileo was one of the first people to point a telescope at the night sky, in 1609.

q: What is the name for the path one object takes around another in space?
fact: Planets' orbits are not perfect circles but slightly squashed ovals called ellipses.

q: What do we call the Moon when its whole face is lit up?
fact: There is a full moon roughly once every 29 and a half days.

q: What is the name for an astronaut from Russia?
fact: Chinese astronauts are sometimes called taikonauts, from the Chinese word for space.

q: What is Earth's only natural satellite?
fact: The Moon is very slowly drifting away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.

q: What are the bowl-shaped dents on the Moon's surface called?
fact: Most of the Moon's craters were made by asteroids and comets crashing into it.

q: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: Earth moving away from the Sun
fact: At the equator, Earth's surface spins at more than 1,600 kilometres per hour.

q: The Moon's gravity is the main cause of what on Earth?
fact: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides roughly every day.

q: What special outfit do astronauts wear to survive outside their spacecraft?
fact: A spacesuit is like a mini spacecraft, supplying oxygen and keeping the wearer at a safe temperature.

q: What is the name for the thin, curved shape the Moon sometimes appears as?
fact: Sunlight bounced off Earth, called earthshine, can make the dark part of a crescent moon faintly glow.

q: What name is given to the Sun and all the planets that travel around it?
fact: 'Solar' comes from 'sol', the Latin word for the Sun.

q: What does UFO stand for?
fact: Before the term UFO caught on, mystery objects in the sky were often called 'flying saucers'.

q: Moonlight is really light reflected from what?
fact: The Moon's surface is actually quite dark, reflecting only about 12% of the sunlight that hits it.

q: What is the layer of gases surrounding Earth called?
fact: The air we breathe is mostly nitrogen, with oxygen making up about a fifth.

q: Apollo astronauts planted which country's flag on the Moon?
fact: With no wind or rain on the Moon, the astronauts' footprints could last for millions of years.

q: What is the name for a huge group of billions of stars, like the Milky Way?
fact: The Andromeda Galaxy is so far away that its light takes over two million years to reach us.

q: What is the Moon mainly made of?
fact: Many scientists think the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized object hit the young Earth.

q: Which of these is classed as a dwarf planet?
fact: Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon.

q: What vehicle is used to launch astronauts into space?
fact: A rocket blasts hot gas out of its back end, which pushes the rocket the opposite way.

q: What is the capital city of Scotland?
fact: Edinburgh Castle sits on top of an extinct volcano known as Castle Rock.

q: What is the capital city of Wales?
fact: Cardiff only became a city in 1905 and was named the capital of Wales in 1955.

q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
fact: Belfast's giant yellow shipyard cranes are nicknamed Samson and Goliath.

q: Which river flows through the centre of London?
fact: The Thames once froze so solidly that 'frost fairs' were held on the ice.

q: The bell known as Big Ben hangs in a tower at which London building?
fact: Big Ben weighs more than 13 tonnes and began striking the hours in 1859.

q: Which London palace is the monarch's official London home?
fact: Buckingham Palace has 775 rooms, including 78 bathrooms.

q: Which vegetable is a national emblem of Wales?
fact: Many people in Wales wear a leek or a daffodil on St David's Day, 1 March.

q: Which prickly purple flower is the national emblem of Scotland?
fact: A thistle appears on the badge of Scotland's national rugby team.

q: Which flower is the national emblem of England?
fact: England's rugby team wears a red rose on its shirts.

q: What colour are London's famous double-decker buses?
fact: The classic Routemaster bus first carried London passengers in 1956.

q: What is the London Underground's famous nickname?
fact: Opened in 1863, the London Underground is the world's oldest underground railway.

q: What is the name of the giant observation wheel on London's South Bank?
fact: The London Eye was built to celebrate the new millennium and opened to the public in 2000.

q: Which creature appears on the national flag of Wales?
fact: Wales isn't represented on the Union Flag, as it was already joined to England when the flag was created.

q: Which London stadium hosts England football matches and the FA Cup Final?
fact: The giant arch over the new Wembley Stadium is 133 metres high.

q: What is the UK's flag commonly called?
fact: The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick.

q: Which northern English city is home to both United and City football clubs?
fact: Manchester's symbol, the worker bee, celebrates the city's busy industrial past.

q: Which stretch of sea separates England from France?
fact: At its narrowest point, the Strait of Dover, the Channel is only about 33 kilometres wide.

q: Which train service runs through the Channel Tunnel from London to Paris?
fact: Eurostar trains leave London from St Pancras International station.

q: The famous White Cliffs stand beside which Kent port?
fact: The White Cliffs are made of chalk, formed from the remains of tiny sea creatures.

q: Which stretch of sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
fact: The Isle of Man sits in the middle of the Irish Sea.

q: What is the knee-length tartan garment traditionally worn by Scottish men?
fact: Many tartan patterns are linked to a particular Scottish clan or family.

q: Which musical instrument is most closely linked with Scotland?
fact: Bagpipes get their sound from a bag of air squeezed under the player's arm.

q: Which Scottish dish is traditionally eaten on Burns Night?
fact: Burns Night celebrates the poet Robert Burns, who wrote a poem called 'Address to a Haggis'.

q: In which university city can you go punting on the River Cam?
fact: Cambridge's Mathematical Bridge is a famous wooden footbridge over the River Cam.

q: What are the ceremonial guards at the Tower of London popularly called?
fact: Officially called Yeoman Warders, Beefeaters live with their families inside the Tower.

q: Which birds are famously kept at the Tower of London?
fact: Legend says the kingdom will fall if the ravens ever leave the Tower.

q: Which London area is famous for its theatres and musicals?
fact: The site of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, has had a theatre on it since 1663.

q: Which London museum is famous for its dinosaur skeletons?
fact: A blue whale skeleton nicknamed Hope hangs in the Natural History Museum's main hall.

q: Which ceremony outside Buckingham Palace sees soldiers in bearskin hats swap duty?
fact: The Changing of the Guard is free to watch and draws big crowds of visitors.

q: Which national park in Cumbria is famous for its lakes and fells?
fact: England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, is in the Lake District.

q: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
fact: A mountain railway has carried visitors up Yr Wyddfa since 1896.

q: Which Somerset festival is one of the world's most famous music festivals?
fact: Glastonbury Festival takes place on a working dairy farm called Worthy Farm.

q: Which Lancashire seaside town is famous for its tower and illuminations?
fact: Blackpool Tower was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and opened in 1894.

q: Which East Sussex seaside city is famous for its pier and Royal Pavilion?
fact: Brighton's Royal Pavilion was built as a seaside palace for the Prince Regent, later King George IV.

q: Which Yorkshire city is famous for its great Minster and old city walls?
fact: The Shambles in York is a narrow medieval street once lined with butchers' shops.
